slides.headline: One park went from 12 rhinos to 2,613.
slides.sub: How the greater one-horned rhino came back from the edge

slides.headline: Around 1900, Kaziranga had 12 rhinos
slides.body: Today Kaziranga National Park in Assam holds an estimated 2,613, the largest population of the species.

slides.headline: It once roamed the northern plains
slides.body: The species ranged from the Indus valley to Assam. Hunting and the clearing of floodplain grasslands for farming wiped most of it out.

slides.headline: Protection worked
slides.body: Numbers recover quickly when floodplain grasslands, and the rhinos themselves, are protected from poaching. IUCN puts 91–100% of them inside protected areas.

slides.label: greater one-horned rhinos by March 2025
slides.body: An estimated 3,323 in India and 752 in Nepal. Kaziranga alone holds 2,613 of them.
slides.source: IUCN SSC rhino specialist groups and TRAFFIC (2025)

slides.headline: Recovered, but still Vulnerable
slides.body: IUCN lists it as Vulnerable (assessed 2018), population increasing. But it survives at just 11 sites, and poaching for horn has not stopped.

slides.headline: Save this proof that protection works.
slides.body: One park, 12 rhinos, a century of protection. Follow @earthspirit_nature.

caption:
Around 1900, Kaziranga had about 12 greater one-horned rhinos (Rhinoceros unicornis). Today it has an estimated 2,613.

Nepal went through the same collapse and recovery. Chitwan's rhinos fell to 60–80 animals in the late 1960s, then climbed back past 600 by 2015. Rhinos from recovered parks have since been moved to reserves where the species had died out.

Swipe to see how it happened. Sources on the last slide.

Source: IUCN Red List (assessed 2018); IUCN SSC rhino specialist groups and TRAFFIC (2025); Britannica; Animal Diversity Web.
